stem.text: Porphyria is a group of rare genetic diseases in which molecules called porphyrins accumulate in the body.
Three examples of porphyria are:
X-linked protoporphyria is caused by a mutant allele located on the X chromosome.
Fig. 3.1 shows the pattern of inheritance of X-linked protoporphyria in one family.
X-linked protoporphyria is described as a sex-linked disease.
Use the information in Fig. 3.1 to make one other conclusion about the pattern of inheritance of X-linked protoporphyria.
Give evidence to support your conclusion.

points.text: 3 / daughter, has disease but, 2 / father, does not or
3 / daughter, could not have the disease if allele were recessive ;

explanation.text: Each gamete carries one allele at each locus. Combine one gamete from each parent, then apply the dominance and sex-linkage rules to determine phenotype.

reasoningChain: Write parental genotypes and all possible gametes.
Combine gametes and count the requested genotypes or phenotypes.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing diploid allele pairs as gametes

stem.text: Variegate porphyria occurs in 1 in 100 000 people in Europe.
In the 1600s, approximately 100 Dutch people migrated from Europe to South Africa.
The population of people of Dutch descent in South Africa is now 2.5 million. Variegate porphyria occurs in 1 in 1000 people in this population.
Suggest and explain why variegate porphyria is more common among people of Dutch descent in South Africa than among people in Europe.

points.text: 1 founder effect ;
2 allele / variegate porphyria, present in, migrants / settlers / founding population ;
3 higher frequency than in, Dutch / Europeans / original population ;
4 genetic drift has large effect in small, population / gene pool ;
5 inbreeding / migrants married within their own population ;
6 high frequency of allele maintained over, time / generations ;

explanation.text: Drift is a chance change in allele frequencies and has greater relative effects in small populations. A founder event or bottleneck samples only part of the original gene pool.

reasoningChain: Identify the change in population size or founding sample.
Trace random allele sampling to the later gene pool.

inferredMistakes.text: Attributing all allele-frequency change to natural selection

stem.text: Microarrays can be used to detect various forms of porphyria caused by mutant alleles.
Describe how microarrays can be used to detect a disease by analysing gene expression.

points.text: 1 use mRNA (from person’s cells) to make, cDNA / ssDNA ;
2 add fluorescent, label / tag / dye / chemical / marker, to (this ss) DNA ;
3 cDNA / ssDNA, hybridises with / binds to / complementary base pairs with, probe(s) / microarray ;
4 fluorescence shows, disease / mutant, gene / allele, expression / transcription ;

explanation.text: Microarrays detect complementary sequence binding. For expression studies, labelled cDNA made from mRNA indicates which genes were transcribed in the sampled cells.

reasoningChain: Identify the nucleic acid taken from the sample.
Connect complementary binding and fluorescence to gene expression.

inferredMistakes.text: Equating the presence of a genomic allele with evidence that it is expressed

stem.text: The nucleotide sequences of alleles that cause rare genetic diseases, such as the various forms of porphyria, are stored in a database.
State one benefit of having a database of nucleotide sequences for alleles that cause rare diseases.

points.text: 1 find out / diagnose, person’s disease ;
2 so can, choose / develop, right treatment ;
3 global, research resource / access ;

explanation.text: Sequence databases allow comparisons across samples and organisms. Their value comes from shared reference information and analysis, rather than directly changing a patient’s DNA.

reasoningChain: Explain how access to the comparison supports research, diagnosis or treatment choice.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing a database as a treatment that directly corrects a mutation

stem.text: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) is caused by a substitution mutation in a gene coding for an enzyme.
The mutant CEP allele codes for an enzyme with little or no function.
Scientists used gene editing in the laboratory to correct the nucleotide sequence of the mutant allele in cultured human cells.
The scientists introduced three molecules to the cells:

items: an enzyme called Cas9 that causes breaks in DNA strands
guide RNA (gRNA), attached to Cas9, that is complementary to the mutant CEP allele
a short length of DNA, known as template DNA, that can replace the section of the allele where the substitution mutation has occurred.

stem.text: The repair mechanism within the cell allows the template DNA to be inserted so that the mutation is corrected.
Fig. 3.2 shows part of the nucleotide sequence in the mutated CEP allele before and after the gene editing procedure.
In the future, this gene editing procedure may be used in a person with CEP to prevent the accumulation of porphyrins in the body.
Suggest and explain how this gene editing procedure will prevent the accumulation of porphyrins in a person with CEP without damaging other genes.

points.text: 1 change from T to C or replacement / substitution, of T, with / by, C or substitution of C for T ;
2 functional / working / correct / normal, enzyme / protein, produced ;
3 gRNA, is specific to / only finds / just alters, CEP /disease / mutant, allele / gene or gRNA does not bind to genes other than CEP ;

explanation.text: Gene editing targets a specified genomic site. A guide sequence provides specificity, while a supplied repair template can direct replacement of the altered base sequence.

reasoningChain: Identify the sequence difference to be corrected.
Connect targeting, cutting and repair to the intended functional product.

inferredMistakes.text: Confusing targeted editing with random insertion of an unrelated gene
